title: The Core Facilitator must recuse on conflict of interest, and resolve any doubt by recusing
content:
Two short Core documents complete the accountability circuit around the adjudicator. A.1.5.9.4: if the Core Facilitator is themselves the subject of a misalignment or opsec allegation, "the adjudication process may be initiated by Core GovOps." A.1.5.9.5: "If the Core Facilitator is subject to a conflict of interest in resolving a dispute, then the Core Facilitator should recuse itself and the adjudication should be conducted by Core GovOps. In cases of doubt, the Core Facilitator should resolve the doubt by recusing itself."

The tie-breaking instruction is the substantive part. Conflict of interest is rarely clear-cut, and the party best placed to assess it is the conflicted party — who has every incentive to find the conflict insufficient. Pre-setting the default removes that judgment call: ambiguity produces recusal automatically, and a facilitator who stayed on a doubtful case has violated the rule regardless of how the case came out.

Read against A.1.5.9.0.4.2, the Atlas is applying the same technique in opposite directions. Doubt about an accused AC's alignment is "resolved against them"; doubt about the facilitator's own impartiality is resolved against the facilitator continuing. Both defaults point away from the party holding power in the moment, and both remove discretion precisely where self-interest would otherwise operate.

The structural requirement this depends on is a standing alternate. Recusal is only available if someone else can adjudicate, and naming Core GovOps in advance means recusal never creates a vacuum — which is what usually makes recusal rules unusable in small governance bodies.
description: A.1.5.9.5 hands the adjudication to Core GovOps on recusal and sets the default toward stepping aside — the mirror image of the rule resolving doubt against an accused AC.
